chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
He used to forbid the walnuts from being eaten when the children used to bring them from the gambling, and he said: 'It is an ill-gotten gain (suh't).'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on eating walnuts brought from gambling in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) specifically prohibited consuming walnuts brought by children from gambling games, declaring them 'suh't' (ill-gotten gain), which highlights the transmission of impurity from the source of acquisition to the object itself. This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle that goods acquired through unlawful means like gambling are tainted, rendering their consumption impermissible even if the item itself is naturally pure. The mention of children emphasizes that the impurity attaches to the goods regardless of the consumer's status, serving as a practical lesson in economic ethics.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Al Nowfaly, from Sakuny, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup>, said, ‘He<sup>asws</sup>
used to fobid from the walnuts to be eaten when the children used to come with these from the gambling, and said: ‘It is an ill-gotten gain’.
en.sarwar: 5. Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Safwan from al-‘Ala’ from Muhammad ibn Muslim who has said the following: “One of the two Imam, (abu Ja’far or abu ‘Abd Allah), ‘Alayhim al-Salam, has said, ‘Gambling and plundering are not righteous deeds.’”
